READING: 'stress usually falls on the last long vowel' = rightmost long vowel attracts stress, stated as a tendency with no default fo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress tends to fall on the rightmost long vowel of the word (i.e. a final long vowel is normally stressed); stated as a tendency ('usually'), with no rule given for words lacking long vowels. Morgenstierne 1967 (SW group, sec.1,15, snippet access only) words it as 'A final long vowel generally carries the stress, but there are many exceptions in the texts which may be due to inexact notation', adds that in numeral groups the second numeral is stressed and that stressed syllables usually carry high tone, with a low rising tone in words with historical voiced aspirates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Grjunberg. Morgenstierne 1944 (Texts, transcription note, snippet): 'In a few cases secondary stress has been noted in polysyllabics (ˈādamana 'by the men')'; Strand's Degano (SE) phoneme table lists a secondary pitch accent as phonemic.
new_statements.exceptions: Grjunberg: 'usually'. Morgenstierne: 'many exceptions in the texts which may be due to inexact notation'; numeral groups stress the second member; emphatic extra-strong stress with high tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; language-level sketch of Pashai as a whole whose phonological data are from the south-western zone. For SE Pashayi proper the primary sources (Lamuwal & Baker 2013; Strand 2005/2012) mark or defer accent rather than state a rule, and both Grjunberg and Morgenstierne flag an aspiration-linked tone specifically in the SE dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Grjunberg 1999) is a language-level sketch of Pashai as a whole (Glottolog subfamily pash1270, four dialect groups); its segment inventories in sec.2.1.1 are explicitly those of the SOUTH-WESTERN zone, and the stress line paraphrases Morgenstierne 1967's SW-group paragraph 1,15 ('A final long vowel generally carries the stress'). It is not a description of Southeast Pashayi (sout2672) specifically. The two first-hand sources on SE Pashayi proper do not give a placement rule: Lamuwal & Baker 2013 (JIPA, Dara-i-Nur) explicitly leave prosody undescribed, and Strand 2005/2012 (Degano dialect of Goraik, Kuz Kunar, also within psi) treats primary/secondary pitch accent as phonemic and writes it lexically. Grjunberg sec.2.1.3 adds, specifically for the south-eastern dialects, a possible aspiration-linked rising tone. Lehr 2014 (UChicago PhD, Darra-i Nur) is the SE-specific grammar that would supersede this.

tone_statements.citation: Morgenstierne, Georg. 1932. Report on a Linguistic Mission to North-Western India. (Instituttet for Sammenlignende Kulturforskning, Serie C III-1.) Oslo: H. Aschehoug & Co. 76 pp. + maps (Pashai dialect survey pp. 21-24).
tone_statements.quote: In some of the Pash. dialects the aspiration of tenues is retained, in others kh results in x, h. In others, again, no aspiration is actually heard; but it has left a trace behind in the rising tone of the following vowel, e. g. ... sir 'milk' ... Similarly after original aspirated media, e. g. Qala-i-Shahid da'r 'hill' < *dhàra-, dar 'wood' < dàru-. (p. 24) ... Aspiration of mediae is not heard in Bashk., but it has left a trace in the low, rising tone, as is the case in Pashai and in Khowar. (p. 30)
tone_statements.locator: p. 24 (Pashai dialect survey, pp. 21-24) and p. 30 (Bashkarik)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: A rising (low-rising) tone on the vowel following a de-aspirated consonant (both old voiceless aspirates and old voiced aspirates) in those Pashai dialects that have lost audible aspiration; other dialects keep aspiration (or kh > x, h) and by implication lack the tone; tonogenesis-by-aspiration-loss remark only, no count of tones, TBU or stress interaction given.

sources.note: In discussing the loss of voiced aspiration across Dardic, Morgenstierne states that in the Pashai dialects the situation varies a good deal, but generally either at least a faint aspiration remains or its place is indicated by a special tone (p. 298) - an early first-hand report of aspiration-replacing (tonogenetic) tone in Pashai, the observation later relayed by Grjunberg 1999 and Baart 2014.
